claim: Hepatocyte-specific deficiency of RIPK1 sensitized the liver to short-term fasting-induced liver injury in both male and female mice.
source: Our results demonstrated that hepatocyte-specific deficiency of RIPK1 sensitized the liver to short-term fasting-induced liver injury and hepatocyte apoptosis in both male and female mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents serum transaminase data (ALT/AST) showing increased liver injury in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting in both male and female mice (Figure 1A, B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-F).

claim: Short-term fasting triggered hepatic inflammation in Ripk1-hepKO mice.
source: Despite being a common physiological stressor that typically does not induce liver inflammation, short-term fasting triggered hepatic inflammation and compensatory proliferation in hepatocyte-specific RIPK1-deficient (Ripk1-hepKO) mice.
evidence: The manuscript shows elevated expression of inflammatory markers (Ccl2, Tnfa, Ifng, Il6) in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 2A).

claim: Short-term fasting triggered compensatory proliferation in Ripk1-hepKO mice.
source: Despite being a common physiological stressor that typically does not induce liver inflammation, short-term fasting triggered hepatic inflammation and compensatory proliferation in hepatocyte-specific RIPK1-deficient (Ripk1-hepKO) mice.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates increased expression of proliferation markers (Afp, Mki67) and increased MKI67-positive cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 2D-G).

claim: Transcriptomic analysis revealed that short-term fasting oriented the hepatic microenvironment into an inflammatory state in Ripk1-hepKO mice.
source: Transcriptomic analysis revealed that short-term fasting oriented the hepatic microenvironment into an inflammatory state in Ripk1-hepKO mice, with up-regulated expression of inflammation and immune cell recruitment-associated genes.
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data showing upregulation of inflammation-associated genes and pathways in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 3A-C).

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing confirmed the altered cellular composition in the liver of Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing further confirmed the altered cellular composition in the liver of Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting, highlighting the increased recruitment of macrophages to the liver.
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNA-seq data showing increased numbers of macrophages and NK&T cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 4A-B).

claim: ER stress was involved in fasting-induced liver injury in Ripk1-hepKO mice.
source: Mechanically, our results indicated that ER stress was involved in fasting-induced liver injury in Ripk1-hepKO mice.
evidence: The manuscript shows that 4-PBA (ER stress inhibitor) treatment reduced liver injury, apoptosis, and inflammation in fasted Ripk1-hepKO mice (Figure 5C-H).

claim: The liver exhibits strong adaptability to maintain homeostasis in response to food fluctuations throughout evolution.
source: As a central hub for metabolism, the liver exhibits strong adaptability to maintain homeostasis in response to food fluctuations throughout evolution.
evidence: This is a general statement about liver function supported by the cited literature (Bernardo-Seisdedos et al., 2021).

claim: Acute fasting triggers hepatic glycogen depletion, increased production of hepatic glucose and ketone bodies, adipose tissue lipolysis, and the influx and accumulation of lipids in the liver.
source: Acute fasting, as one of the main causes of metabolic stress, is known to trigger hepatic glycogen depletion, increased production of hepatic glucose and ketone bodies, adipose tissue lipolysis, and the influx and accumulation of lipids in the liver (Inokuchi-Shimizu et al., 2014; Petersen et al., 2017; Zoncu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Inokuchi-Shimizu et al., 2014; Petersen et al., 2017; Zoncu et al., 2011).

claim: Under normal circumstances, the liver possesses the capability to shield itself from hepatic lipotoxicity caused by the elevated lipid influx and accumulation during fasting.
source: Under normal circumstances, the liver possesses the capability to shield itself from hepatic lipotoxicity caused by the elevated lipid influx and accumulation during fasting (Cotter et al., 2014; Fromenty and Roden, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Cotter et al., 2014; Fromenty and Roden, 2023).

claim: RIPK1 is a crucial mediator of cell death and inflammation.
source: The serine/threonine kinase RIPK1 is a crucial mediator of cell death and inflammation (Mifflin et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Mifflin et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2023).

claim: RIPK1 manifests two distinct functions: its scaffold function regulates cell survival and activation of NF-κB pathway, while its kinase activity promotes cell death including apoptosis and necroptosis.
source: It manifests two distinct, even opposing functions: its scaffold function regulates cell survival and activation of NF-κB pathway, while its kinase activity promotes cell death including apoptosis and necroptosis (Clucas and Meier, 2023; Ofengeim and Yuan, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Clucas and Meier, 2023; Ofengeim and Yuan, 2013).

claim: The kinase activity of RIPK1 has been extensively studied due to its association with deleterious effects in pathological situations.
source: Notably, the kinase activity of RIPK1 has been extensively studied due to its association with the deleterious effects in pathological situations (Majdi et al., 2020; Tao et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021; Yin et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Majdi et al., 2020; Tao et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021; Yin et al., 2022).

claim: The scaffold function of RIPK1 plays an essential role in maintaining tissue homeostasis within physiological context.
source: In contrast, the scaffold function of RIPK1 is less studied and current evidences suggest that it plays an essential role in maintaining tissue homeostasis within physiological context (Mei et al., 2021; Najafov et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Mei et al., 2021; Najafov et al., 2021).

claim: The postnatality death of Ripk1−/− mice suggested that the scaffold function of RIPK1 plays an essential role in normal development.
source: The postnatality death of Ripk1−/− mice suggested that the scaffold function of RIPK1 plays an essential role in normal development, acting as a brake to prevent cell death and inflammation in different tissues (Kelliher et al., 1998; Rickard et al., 2014; Silke et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kelliher et al., 1998; Rickard et al., 2014; Silke et al., 2015).

claim: Mice lacking RIPK1 in hepatocytes (Ripk1-hepKO) exhibit a state of health and normal under steady conditions.
source: In contrast to the severe phenotype observed in mice with RIPK1 deletion in epithelial cells, mice lacking RIPK1 in hepatocytes (Ripk1-hepKO) exhibit a surprising state of health and normal under steady conditions (Dannappel et al., 2014; Filliol et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Dannappel et al., 2014; Filliol et al., 2016) and confirmed by the current study's observations.

claim: When confronted with pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) or viral challenges, Ripk1-hepKO mice display heightened inflammation and cell death.
source: Nonetheless, when confronted with pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) or viral challenges, Ripk1-hepKO mice display heightened inflammation and cell death (Farooq et al., 2019; Filliol et al., 2017; Filliol et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Farooq et al., 2019; Filliol et al., 2017; Filliol et al., 2016).

claim: Short-term fasting induced a significant increase in serum transaminase (ALT and AST) levels in Ripk1-hepKO mice but not in their wild-type controls.
source: To our surprise, short-term fasting induced a significant increase in serum transaminase (alanine amino-transferase (ALT) and aspartate amino-transferase (AST)) levels in Ripk1-hepKO mice but not in their wild-type controls, suggesting that RIPK1 deficiency sensitizes the liver to short-term fasting, inducing acute liver injury (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing elevated ALT and AST levels in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 1A, B).

claim: The number of TUNEL-positive cells in the liver of Ripk1-hepKO mice was significantly higher compared to the control mice after fasting.
source: As Figure 1C, D shown, the number of TUNEL-positive cells in the liver of Ripk1-hepKO mice was significantly higher compared to the control mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents TUNEL staining data showing increased apoptotic cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 1C, D).

claim: The number of cleaved caspase-3-positive cells was significantly higher in Ripk1-hepKO mice compared to controls after fasting.
source: As indicated in Figure 1E, F, the number of cleaved caspase-3-positive cells was significantly higher in Ripk1-hepKO mice compared to controls.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing increased cleaved caspase-3-positive cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 1E, F).

claim: There was no change in the number of phospho-MLKL-positive cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting.
source: In contrast, we did not observe any change in the number of phospho-MLKL-positive cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice (Figure 1G).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing no change in phospho-MLKL-positive cells (Figure 1G).

claim: Fasting-induced acute liver injury in Ripk1-hepKO mice is due to apoptosis rather than necroptosis.
source: These results suggest that fasting-induced acute liver injury in Ripk1-hepKO mice might be due to apoptosis rather than necroptosis.
evidence: The manuscript shows increased cleaved caspase-3 (apoptosis marker) but not phospho-MLKL (necroptosis marker) in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting.

claim: Most TUNEL-positive cells co-localized with Alb-positive staining in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting.
source: To further investigate which cell types were undergoing apoptosis, we conducted the co-staining with TUNEL and Alb immunofluorescence, and the results demonstrated that most of TUNEL-positive cells co-localized with Alb-positive staining (Figure 1H), suggesting that short-term fasting-induced apoptosis mainly in hepatic parenchymal cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents co-staining data showing overlap between TUNEL and Alb staining (Figure 1H).

claim: Short-term fasting-induced apoptosis mainly in hepatic parenchymal cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice.
source: To further investigate which cell types were undergoing apoptosis, we conducted the co-staining with TUNEL and Alb immunofluorescence, and the results demonstrated that most of TUNEL-positive cells co-localized with Alb-positive staining (Figure 1H), suggesting that short-term fasting-induced apoptosis mainly in hepatic parenchymal cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents co-staining data showing overlap between TUNEL and Alb staining (Figure 1H), indicating apoptosis in hepatocytes.

claim: RIPK1 deficiency did not affect the lipid metabolism in liver during fasting.
source: As Figure 1I–O shown, short-term fasting significantly decreased the blood glucose level, elevated the plasma levels of triglycerides (TG), total cholesterol (TC), FFA, β-hydroxybutyrate, and hepatic TG, and there was no obvious difference between wild-type control and Ripk1-hepKO mice, suggesting that RIPK1 deficiency did not affect the lipid metabolism in liver during fasting.
evidence: The manuscript presents metabolic parameter data showing no significant differences between Ripk1-Con and Ripk1-hepKO mice in blood glucose, TG, TC, FFA, β-hydroxybutyrate, and hepatic TG levels during fasting (Figure 1I-O).

claim: Female Ripk1-hepKO mice showed a significant increase in serum ALT/AST levels and hepatic TUNEL-positive cells after short-term fasting.
source: Consistent with male mice, we observed a significant increase in serum ALT/AST levels and hepatic TUNEL-positive cells in Ripk1-hepKO female mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–F), suggesting that RIPK1 deficiency sensitizes the liver to short-term fasting-induced liver injury and hepatocyte apoptosis in both male and female mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from female mice showing elevated ALT/AST and TUNEL-positive cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-F).

claim: Short-term fasting did not cause acute liver injury in Ripk1-K45A mice.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B, we observed no increase in serum ALT/AST levels in Ripk1-K45A mice after 12 hr of fasting, suggesting that short-term fasting did not cause acute liver injury in these mice, unlike in Ripk1-hepKO mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing no elevation in ALT/AST levels in Ripk1-K45A mice after fasting (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).

claim: The inactivation of RIPK1 kinase does not affect lipid metabolism in the liver during fasting.
source: Additionally, short-term fasting resulted in elevated plasma levels of TG, TC, and hepatic TG, with no significant differences between wild-type controls and Ripk1-K45A mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E). This suggests that the inactivation of RIPK1 kinase does not affect lipid metabolism in the liver during fasting and this was consistent with Ripk1-hepKO mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents metabolic data showing no differences between wild-type and Ripk1-K45A mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-E).

claim: The transcriptional expression of inflammatory markers (Ccl2, Tnfa, Ifng, and Il6) was significantly induced in Ripk1-hepKO mouse liver tissue after fasting.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 2A, the transcriptional expression of inflammatory markers, including Ccl2, Tnfa, Ifng, and Il6, was all significantly induced in Ripk1-hepKO mouse liver tissue, in contrast to wild-type littermates.
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing elevated expression of inflammatory markers in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 2A).

claim: There was a significant increase in the expression of Afp and Mki67 in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting.
source: We also evaluated the expression of Afp, a marker gene of hepatocellular carcinoma, and Mki67, a proliferation-related antigen, and found a significant increase in both markers in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing increased expression of Afp and Mki67 in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 2D).

claim: There was a significant increase in the number of MKI67-positive cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice after 12 hr of fasting.
source: To validate these findings at the protein level, we used immunohistochemistry of MKI67 to measure the rate of compensatory proliferation in livers and found a significant increase in the number of MKI67-positive cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice after 12 hr of fasting when liver injury was detected (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunohistochemistry data showing increased MKI67-positive cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 2E).

claim: Flow cytometric analysis revealed a significant increase in the number of MKI67-positive cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice compared to control mice after 12 hr of fasting.
source: Similarly, flow cytometric analysis of liver tissue from mice after 12 hr of fasting also revealed a significant increase in the number of MKI67-positive cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice compared to control mice (Figure 2F, G).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing increased MKI67-positive cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 2F, G).

claim: No changes were observed in the transcriptional expression of inflammatory markers or compensatory proliferation markers in the liver tissue of Ripk1-K45A mice during fasting.
source: In contrast, no changes were observed in the transcriptional expression of inflammatory markers (Ccl2, Tnfa, Ifng, and Il6) or compensatory proliferation markers (Afp and Mki67) in the liver tissue of Ripk1-K45A mice during fasting (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, G).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing no changes in inflammatory or proliferation markers in Ripk1-K45A mice during fasting (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, G).

claim: Fasting significantly remodeled the transcriptional expression of various genes associated with metabolism in wild-type mice, with 454 genes up-regulated and 545 genes down-regulated.
source: Consistent with previous reports, fasting significantly remodeled the transcriptional expression of various genes associated with metabolism in wild-type mice, among which 454 genes were up-regulated and 545 genes were down-regulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data showing differentially expressed genes in wild-type mice during fasting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Differentially expressed genes in wild-type mice during fasting were primarily enriched in metabolism-associated pathways, including fatty acid degradation, PPAR signaling pathway and MAPK signaling pathway.
source: As expected, pathway enrichment (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes, KEGG) analysis revealed that these differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were primarily enriched in metabolism-associated pathways, including fatty acid degradation, PPAR signaling pathway and MAPK signaling pathway (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript presents KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of DEGs in wild-type mice during fasting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: In wild-type mice, fasting normally suppressed the expression of immune- or inflammation-related genes.
source: To be noteworthy, in wild-type mice, fasting normally suppressed the expression of immune- or inflammation-related genes, in agreement with the shifted energy to guarantee the need for basic survival other than immune protection during food deprivation.
evidence: This claim is based on the transcriptomic analysis presented in the manuscript and is consistent with established knowledge about metabolic prioritization during fasting.

claim: RIPK1 deficiency in hepatocytes did not greatly affect the gene expression profiles when food was available.
source: RIPK1 deficiency in hepatocytes did not greatly affect the gene expression profiles when food was available and there were 25 up-regulated and 54 down-regulated genes which were mostly associated with alcoholic liver disease, vascular smooth muscle contraction and cardiomyopathy in Ripk1-hepKO mice compared to wild-type control at fed state (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data showing minimal changes in gene expression in Ripk1-hepKO mice at fed state (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).

claim: Loss of RIPK1 in hepatocytes during fasting resulted in 85 up-regulated and 29 down-regulated genes compared to the Ripk1-Con group.
source: However, when subjected to metabolic fluctuation with short-term fasting, loss of RIPK1 in hepatocytes amplified the affect, and there were additional 85 up-regulated and 29 down-regulated genes identified in Ripk1-hepKO mice compared to the Ripk1-Con group (p < 0.05, |log2(fold change)| ≥ 1) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript presents RNA-seq data showing differentially expressed genes in Ripk1-hepKO mice compared to controls during fasting (Figure 3A).

claim: Differentially expressed genes in Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting were primarily enriched in inflammation-associated pathways, including TNF signaling pathway, IL-17 signaling pathway, toll-like receptor signaling pathway, NF-κB signaling pathway.
source: Pathway enrichment (KEGG) analysis revealed that these DEGs were primarily enriched in inflammation-associated pathways, including TNF signaling pathway, IL-17 signaling pathway, toll-like receptor signaling pathway, NF-κB signaling pathway, etc. (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of DEGs in Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting (Figure 3B).

claim: Hepatocyte-specific deletion of RIPK1 significantly induced the expression of many genes involved in the inflammatory process after fasting, including Ccl2, Clec4e, Ikbke, Tnfaip3.
source: Cluster analysis of the DEGs revealed that hepatocyte-specific deletion of RIPK1 significantly induced the expression of many genes involved in the inflammatory process after fasting, including Ccl2, Clec4e, Ikbke, Tnfaip3, etc. (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript presents a heatmap showing increased expression of inflammatory genes in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 3C).

claim: There was a significant increase in the expression of chemokine-related genes involved in the recruitment of immune cells, such as Itgam, Ccr2, and Cx3cr1, in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting.
source: Through further analysis of the transcriptome data, we observed a significant increase in the expression chemokine-related genes involved in the recruitment of immune cells, such as Itgam, Ccr2, and Cx3cr1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript presents transcriptome data showing increased expression of chemokine-related genes in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 3C).

claim: There was a significant increase in the number of CD11b-, CCR2-, and CX3CR1-positive cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting, while F4/80 expression remained unchanged.
source: To validate these findings at the protein level, we conducted immunofluorescence staining for F4/80, a marker for liver-resident immune cells, and CD11b, CCR2, and CX3CR1, markers for liver-recruited immune cells. Our results demonstrated a significant increase in the number of CD11b-, CCR2-, and CX3CR1-positive cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting, while F4/80 expression remained unchanged (Figure 3D, E).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing increased CD11b-, CCR2-, and CX3CR1-positive cells but unchanged F4/80 expression in Ripk1-hepKO mice after fasting (Figure 3D, E).

claim: RIPK1 deficiency sensitizes the liver into a proinflammatory state during fasting, with induced expression of inflammation and immune cell recruitment-associated genes.
source: These results suggested that in contrast to the immunosuppression state of liver during fasting, RIPK1 deficiency sensitize the liver into a proinflammatory state, with induced expression of inflammation and immune cell recruitment-associated genes.
evidence: This claim is based on the transcriptomic and immunofluorescence data showing increased inflammatory gene expression and immune cell recruitment in Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting.

claim: A total of 22,274 single-cell transcriptomes (10,374 Ripk1-Con; 11,900 Ripk1-hepKO) were obtained from single-cell RNA sequencing of liver non-parenchymal cells.
source: A total of 22,274 single-cell transcriptomes (10,374 Ripk1-Con; 11,900 Ripk1-hepKO) were obtained, and 30 major clusters were identified by T-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) visualization, representing different cell types based on marker gene expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the scRNA-seq data obtained from liver non-parenchymal cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).

claim: Short-term fasting led to significant changes in the cellular composition of the liver in Ripk1-hepKO mice, characterized by an increase in the number of cells in clusters 12, 14, 19, 22, and 28 and a decrease in the number of cells in clusters 9, 11, 22, 26, and 29.
source: As the result shown, short-term fasting led to significant changes in the cellular composition of the liver in Ripk1-hepKO mice, characterized by an increase in the number of cells in clusters 12, 14, 19, 22, and 28 and a decrease in the number of cells in clusters 9, 11, 22, 26, and 29, compared to control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNA-seq data showing changes in cellular composition in Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).

claim: Eight major cellular clusters were identified in 12-hr fasted control liver, including B cells, neutrophils, ECs, PCs, DCs, NK&T cells, macrophages, and hepatocytes.
source: In order to further explore the significance of these changes, we identified eight major cellular clusters in 12-hr fasted control liver, including B cells (Cd19, Cd79a, Fcmr, Cd79b, Ebf1), neutrophils (S100a8, Csf3r, S100a9, Mmp9), ECs (Igfbp7, Ptprb, Clec4g, Kdr), PCs (Sdc1, CD138), DCs (Ly6d, Siglech, Rnase6, H2-Ab1), NK&T cells (Nkg7, Xcl1, Cd3d, Gzma), macrophages (Adgre1, Csf1r, Sdc3, Ifitm2), and hepatocytes (Alb, Saa1, Apoc1, Mup20) (Figure 4A; Sun et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNA-seq data showing eight major cell types identified based on marker gene expression (Figure 4A), with citations to previous literature (Sun et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2020).

claim: The numbers of macrophages and NK&T cells were increased in the liver of Ripk1-hepKO mice compared to Ripk1-Con mice upon short-term fasting.
source: As the result shown, the numbers of macrophages and NK&T cells were increased in the liver of Ripk1-hepKO mice compared to that of Ripk1-Con mice upon short-term fasting, suggesting the dynamics of recruited immune cells into liver in Ripk1-hepKO mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNA-seq data showing increased proportions of macrophages and NK&T cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting (Figure 4B).

claim: Differentially expressed genes in macrophages from Ripk1-hepKO mice were primarily enriched in inflammation-associated pathways, including IL-17 signaling pathway, antigen processing and presentation and TNF signaling pathway.
source: As expected, pathway enrichment (KEGG) analysis based on macrophage differential genes revealed that these DEGs were primarily enriched in inflammation-associated pathways, including IL-17 signaling pathway, antigen processing and presentation and TNF signaling pathway, etc. (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript presents KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of macrophage DEGs (Figure 4C).

claim: Macrophages can be divided into two groups representing liver-resident macrophages (LrMs: KCs) and recruited macrophages (RMs).
source: This cluster can be further divided into two groups of cells representing liver-resident macrophages (LrMs: KCs) and RMs based on their marker gene expression profile (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNA-seq data showing sub-clustering of macrophages into LrMs and RMs (Figure 4D).

claim: LrMs were characterized by high expression of Adgre1 (encoding F4/80) and Clec4f, whereas RMs exhibited high expression of Itgam (encoding Cd11b), Ccr2, and Cx3cr1.
source: LrMs were characterized by high expression of Adgre1 (encoding F4/80) and Clec4f, whereas RMs exhibited high expression of Itgam (encoding Cd11b, an important marker gene of bone marrow-derived macrophages), Ccr2 (a chemokine receptor important for infiltration of circulating monocytes), and Cx3cr1 (Krenkel and Tacke, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the marker gene expression profiles of LrMs and RMs, with a citation to previous literature (Krenkel and Tacke, 2017).

claim: The number of LrMs remained almost unchanged in Ripk1-hepKO mice after short-term fasting compared to Ripk1-Con mice, while the number of RMs significantly increased.
source: We observed that while the number of LrMs remained almost unchanged in Ripk1-hepKO mice after short-term fasting compared to Ripk1-Con mice, the number of RMs significantly increased (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNA-seq data showing increased proportion of RMs but unchanged LrMs in Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting (Figure 4E).

claim: Flow cytometry analysis revealed a significant increase in the proportion of F4/80+CD11b+ cells among all F4/80+ cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice compared to control mice.
source: This was further confirmed by flow cytometry analysis, which revealed a significant increase in the proportion of F4/80+CD11b+ cells among all F4/80+ cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice compared to control mice (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing increased F4/80+CD11b+ cells in Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting (Figure 4F, G).

claim: Both the number of ligand–receptor pairs and the interaction strength among the eight cell types were higher in the liver tissue of Ripk1-hepKO mice compared to control mice.
source: By comparing the information flow of cell–cell communication between Ripk1-Con and Ripk1-hepKO mice, we found that both the number of ligand–receptor pairs and the interaction strength among the eight cell types were higher in the liver tissue of Ripk1-hepKO mice compared to control mice. This was particularly evident in the enhanced crosstalk between macrophages and other cell clusters (Figure 4H–J).
evidence: The manuscript presents CellChat analysis showing increased cell-cell communication in Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting (Figure 4H-J).

claim: Signals between various cell types specifically enriched in Ripk1-hepKO mice were predominantly linked to inflammation-related pathways, such as MHC I, OSM, GAS, and HSPG, as well as proliferation-related pathways including IGF, KIT, NOTCH, and LAMININ.
source: To analyze the detailed communication within individual pathways, we performed a network analysis that was visualized using a heatmap. This heatmap illustrated the signals between various cell types specifically enriched in Ripk1-hepKO mice (Figure 4K). These signals were predominantly linked to inflammation-related pathways, such as MHC I, OSM, GAS, and HSPG, as well as proliferation-related pathways including IGF, KIT, NOTCH, and LAMININ.
evidence: The manuscript presents CellChat analysis showing enriched signaling pathways in Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting (Figure 4K).

claim: Fasting amplified SAA signaling in the hepatocytes of Ripk1-hepKO mice.
source: Interestingly, we discovered that fasting amplified SAA signaling in the hepatocytes of Ripk1-hepKO mice. This increase in SAA signaling was consistent with elevated transcription levels of SAA2, SAA3, and SAA4, as evidenced by liver transcriptome data (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript presents CellChat and transcriptome data showing increased SAA signaling in Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting (Figure 3C, Figure 4K).

claim: SAA released by hepatocytes has been reported to play a role in regulating immune responses and tumor development.
source: The SAA released by hepatocytes has been reported to play a role in regulating immune responses and tumor development (Li et al., 2024; Stone et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Li et al., 2024; Stone et al., 2024).

claim: Fasting-induced liver injury in RIPK1 knockout mice of hepatic parenchymal cells may exacerbate the inflammatory response in liver tissue through enhanced SAA signaling.
source: These above results suggest that fasting-induced liver injury in RIPK1 knockout mice of hepatic parenchymal cells may exacerbate the inflammatory response in liver tissue through enhanced SAA signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on the observed increase in SAA signaling in Ripk1-hepKO mice and the known role of SAA in immune responses.

claim: Short-term fasting increased the expression of CHOP, BIP, IRE1a, and phosphor-IRE1a at protein levels in liver tissue.
source: As Figure 5A indicated, short-term fasting indeed increased the expression of CHOP, BIP, IRE1a, and phosphor-IRE1a at protein levels, suggesting that short-term fasting caused ER stress in liver.
evidence: The manuscript presents Western blot data showing increased expression of ER stress markers during fasting (Figure 5A).

claim: 4-PBA treatment successfully reduced the expression of ER stress markers.
source: As Figure 5C shown, 4-PBA treatment successfully reduced the expression of ER stress markers, confirming the efficiency of 4-PBA to inhibit ER stress.
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing reduced expression of ER stress markers after 4-PBA treatment (Figure 5C).

claim: 4-PBA pretreatment effectively reduced serum ALT/AST levels and the number of TUNEL-positive cells in the liver of fasted Ripk1-hepKO mice.
source: Interestingly, 4-PBA pretreatment effectively reduced serum ALT/AST levels and the number of TUNEL-positive cells in the liver of fasted Ripk1-hepKO mice, suggesting that ER stress was involved in fasting-induced liver injury and hepatocyte apoptosis in Ripk1-hepKO mice (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that 4-PBA treatment reduced liver injury markers in Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting (Figure 5D-F).

claim: 4-PBA pretreatment effectively inhibited the increased expression of inflammatory markers (Ccl2, Tnfa, Ifng, and Il6) and proliferation marker Afp in the liver tissue of fasted Ripk1-hepKO mice.
source: Furthermore, 4-PBA pretreatment also effectively inhibited the increased expression of inflammatory markers (Ccl2, Tnfa, Ifng, and Il6) and proliferation markers Afp in the liver tissue of fasted Ripk1-hepKO mice (Figure 5G, H).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing that 4-PBA treatment reduced inflammatory and proliferation marker expression in Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting (Figure 5G, H).

claim: ER stress was involved in the process of fasting-induced liver injury and inflammation in Ripk1-hepKO mice.
source: These results indicated that 4-PBA not only prevented hepatocyte apoptosis and liver injury induced by fasting in Ripk1-hepKO mice, but also mitigated the hepatic inflammation and compensatory proliferation, suggesting that ER stress was involved in the process of fasting-induced liver injury and inflammation in Ripk1-hepKO mice.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that 4-PBA (ER stress inhibitor) treatment prevented liver injury, apoptosis, and inflammation in Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting.

claim: AAV8-TBG-Cre virus treatment specifically deleted RIPK1 in hepatocytes.
source: Immunoblot analysis confirmed that RIPK1 was specifically deleted in hepatocytes by AAV8-TBG-Cre virus treatment, in contrast to the control virus AAV8-TBG-null (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript presents Western blot data showing deletion of RIPK1 in AAV8-TBG-Cre treated mice (Figure 6B).

claim: AAV8-TBG-Cre virus-induced RIPK1-deficient mice phenocopied Ripk1-hepKO mice, with hepatocyte-specific loss of RIPK1 sensitizing the mice to short-term fasting-induced acute liver injury and hepatocyte apoptosis.
source: Our results indicated that AAV8-TBG-Cre virus-induced RIPK1-deficient mice phenocopied Ripk1-hepKO mice, that hepatocyte-specific loss of RIPK1 sensitized the mice to short-term fasting-induced acute liver injury and hepatocyte apoptosis (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that AAV8-TBG-Cre treated mice exhibited similar phenotypes to Ripk1-hepKO mice during fasting (Figure 6C-F).

claim: There was no significant alteration in serum TG, TC, and liver TG levels of Ripk1-Con mice injected with AAV8-TBG-Cre or control AAV8-TBG-null virus.
source: Consistently, there was no significant alteration in serum TG, TC, and liver TG levels of Ripk1-Con mice injected with AAV8-TBG-Cre or control AAV8-TBG-null virus (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing no differences in lipid metabolism parameters between AAV8-TBG-Cre and AAV8-TBG-null treated mice (Figure 6G-I).

claim: Short-term fasting increased the expression of CHOP (Ddit3), BIP (Hspa5), IRE1α, and phosphor-IRE1α at both mRNA and protein levels in RIPK1-deleted livers.
source: We also detected the expression of ER stress markers in the liver tissue of AAV8-TBG-null or AAV8-TBG-Cre mice, respectively. As Figure 6B, J indicated, short-term fasting indeed increased the expression of CHOP (Ddit3), BIP (Hspa5), IRE1α, and phosphor-IRE1α at both mRNA and protein levels, indicating that fasting induced the occurrence of ER stress in RIPK1-deleted livers.
evidence: The manuscript presents Western blot and qPCR data showing increased ER stress markers in AAV8-TBG-Cre treated mice during fasting (Figure 6B, J).

claim: Transcriptional expression of inflammatory markers, including Ccl2, Tnfa, and Il1b, were significantly induced in AAV8-TBG-Cre-mouse liver tissue after fasting.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 6B, K, transcriptional expression of inflammatory markers, including Ccl2, Tnfa, and Il1b, were also significantly induced in AAV8-TBG-Cre-mouse liver tissue, in contrast to AAV8-TBG-null-mouse.
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing increased inflammatory marker expression in AAV8-TBG-Cre treated mice during fasting (Figure 6B, K).

claim: The number of cleaved caspase-3-positive cells was significantly higher in AAV8-TBG-Cre-mouse compared to controls.
source: Consistent with previous results, the number of cleaved caspase-3-positive cells was significantly higher in AAV8-TBG-Cre-mouse compared to controls (Figure 6L, M).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing increased cleaved caspase-3-positive cells in AAV8-TBG-Cre treated mice during fasting (Figure 6L, M).

claim: Hepatocyte-specific loss of RIPK1, achieved by different strategies, made the mice fragile to metabolic disturbance, with short-term fasting resulting in liver injury, hepatocyte cell death, hepatic inflammation, and ER stress.
source: Taken together, these results suggested that hepatocyte-specific loss of RIPK1, achieved by different strategies, made the mice fragile to metabolic disturbance, and even short-term fasting would result in liver injury, hepatocyte cell death, hepatic inflammation, and ER stress.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings from both Ripk1-hepKO mice and AAV8-TBG-Cre treated mice, showing consistent phenotypes.

claim: Six days of HFD feeding significantly increased liver lipid deposition, liver TG, and serum TC in mice.
source: We observed a significant increase in liver lipid deposition, liver TG, and serum TC in mice fed with HFD compared to those fed with ND (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing increased lipid accumulation in mice fed HFD (Figure 7B-D).

claim: Short-term HFD feeding was not enough to induce hepatic disorder in Ripk1-Con mice, without obvious effects on the serum ALT/AST and liver histology.
source: Previous studies reported that short-term HFD feeding was not enough to induce hepatic disorder, without obvious effects on the serum ALT/AST, liver histology, and our results with Ripk1-Con mice were in agreement with these findings (Figure 7E, F).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing no changes in ALT/AST in Ripk1-Con mice after HFD feeding (Figure 7E, F), consistent with previous literature.

claim: Upon 6-day HFD feeding, the serum ALT/AST levels, hepatocyte apoptosis, and hepatic inflammation were significantly elevated in Ripk1-hepKO mice.
source: In contrast, upon 6-day HFD feeding, the serum ALT/AST levels, hepatocyte apoptosis as measured by TUNEL and hepatic inflammation were significantly elevated in Ripk1-hepKO mice (Figure 7E–I).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing increased liver injury, apoptosis, and inflammation in Ripk1-hepKO mice after HFD feeding (Figure 7E-I).

claim: HFD feeding significantly induced the expression of Afp in Ripk1-hepKO mice.
source: Additionally, HFD feeding significantly induced the expression of Afp in Ripk1-hepKO mice, suggesting that HFD feeding promoted tumorigenesis in Ripk1-hepKO mice (Figure 7J).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing increased Afp expression in Ripk1-hepKO mice after HFD feeding (Figure 7J).

claim: The expression of ER stress-related genes was obviously increased in Ripk1-hepKO mice after 6 days of HFD feeding.
source: We also found that the expression of ER stress-related genes was obviously increased in Ripk1-hepKO mice after 6 days of HFD feeding (Figure 7K).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing increased ER stress marker expression in Ripk1-hepKO mice after HFD feeding (Figure 7K).

claim: Hepatocyte RIPK1 is essential for the maintenance of hepatic homeostasis against the disturbance induced by different metabolism behaviors, including fasting and temporary HFD feeding.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that hepatocyte RIPK1 is essential for the maintenance of hepatic homeostasis against the disturbance induced by different metabolism behaviors, including fasting and temporary HFD feeding.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings from both fasting and HFD feeding experiments, showing that RIPK1 deficiency sensitizes the liver to metabolic challenges.

claim: The specific deletion of RIPK1 in hepatocytes exacerbated the liver's vulnerability to metabolic disturbances, such as short-term fasting and HFD feeding, resulting in increased liver damage, apoptosis, inflammation, and compensatory proliferation.
source: In this study, we demonstrated that the specific deletion of RIPK1 in hepatocytes exacerbated the liver's vulnerability to metabolic disturbances, such as short-term fasting and HFD feeding, resulting in increased liver damage, apoptosis, inflammation, and compensatory proliferation.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study, supported by data from multiple experiments.

claim: RIPK1 has a novel physiological role as a scaffold in maintaining liver homeostasis during fasting and other nutritional disturbance.
source: In summary, we revealed a novel physiological role of RIPK1 as a scaffold in maintaining liver homeostasis during fasting and other nutritional disturbance.
evidence: This claim is based on the findings that RIPK1 deficiency (loss of scaffold function) but not kinase inactivation sensitizes the liver to metabolic challenges.

claim: The pathophysiological roles of RIPK1 have primarily been studied in inflammatory diseases and pathogen infections.
source: While the pathophysiological roles of RIPK1 have primarily been studied in inflammatory diseases and pathogen infections, emerging evidence suggests its involvement in metabolism-related pathways (Mei et al., 2021; Najafov et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Mei et al., 2021; Najafov et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023a).

claim: RIPK1's kinase activity has been linked to the pathogenesis of metabolic diseases like NASH.
source: Previous studies, including our own, have linked RIPK1's kinase activity to the pathogenesis of metabolic diseases like NASH, indicating a metabolic regulatory role of RIPK1 kinase (Majdi et al., 2020; Tao et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Majdi et al., 2020; Tao et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2022).

claim: UDP-glucose 6-dehydrogenase and UDP-glucuronate metabolism suppress NASH pathogenesis and control hepatocyte apoptosis through inhibiting RIPK1 kinase activity.
source: Subsequently, UDP-glucose 6-dehydrogenase and UDP-glucuronate metabolism are found to suppress NASH pathogenesis and control hepatocyte apoptosis through inhibiting RIPK1 kinase activity, further solidifying the connection between RIPK1 kinase activity and metabolism during the pathogenesis of NASH (Zhang et al., 2023b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature (Zhang et al., 2023b).

claim: The postnatal lethality of Ripk1−/− mice was attributed to dysregulated aspartate metabolism, leading to impaired starvation-induced autophagy.
source: Mei et al. found that the postnatal lethality of Ripk1−/− mice was attributed to dysregulated aspartate metabolism, leading to impaired starvation-induced autophagy (Mei et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature (Mei et al., 2021).

claim: AMPK is able to phosphorylate RIPK1 at S416 in response to metabolic stress like glucose deprivation in vitro and fasting in vivo.
source: Zhang et al. recently reported that the classical energy sensor AMPK is able to phosphorylate RIPK1 at S416 in response to metabolic stress like glucose deprivation in vitro and fasting in vivo, and this phosphorylation of RIPK1 by AMPK represents a survival mechanism to keep the kinase activity of RIPK1 in check to prevent RIPK1 kinase-mediated cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature (Zhang et al., 2023a).

claim: AMPK deficiency sensitized cells to glucose deprivation-induced cell death.
source: AMPK deficiency sensitized cells to glucose deprivation-induced cell death (Zhang et al., 2023a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature (Zhang et al., 2023a).

claim: Tak1−/− mice exhibit similar phenotypes to RIPK1-deficient mice.
source: Moreover, Tak1−/− mice has been shown to exhibit similar phenotypes, suggesting that the key components in the complex I faction in the scaffold complex, all contribute to maintain tissue homeostasis (Inokuchi-Shimizu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature (Inokuchi-Shimizu et al., 2014).

claim: RIPK1 knockout MEFs were more susceptible to cell death induced by glucose starvation compared to WT MEFs.
source: Zhang et al. also noted that RIPK1 knockout MEFs (mouse embryonic fibroblasts) were more susceptible to cell death induced by glucose starvation compared to WT MEFs, further underscoring the importance of RIPK1 in nutrient stress responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature (Zhang et al., 2023a).

claim: Deficiencies in TAK1 or NEMO in hepatocytes result in spontaneous liver injury and carcinogenesis in mice, with a more severe phenotype than that observed in RIPK1-deficient mice.
source: Prior investigations have indicated that deficiencies in TAK1 or NEMO in hepatocytes result in spontaneous liver injury and carcinogenesis in mice, with a more severe phenotype than that observed in RIPK1-deficient mice (Bettermann et al., 2010; Luedde et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bettermann et al., 2010; Luedde et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2013).

claim: The deletion of TAK1 or NEMO unleashes the kinase activity of RIPK1, leading to the activation of RIPK1 kinase and the associated cell death pathways.
source: This is attributed to the deletion of TAK1 or NEMO unleashing the kinase activity of RIPK1, leading to the activation of RIPK1 kinase and the associated cell death pathways.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of the RIPK1-TAK1-NEMO signaling axis from previous literature.

claim: The RIPK1–TAK1–NF-κB axis constitutes an essential scaffold platform necessary for the liver's adaptation to metabolic fluctuations.
source: Our findings, combined with these earlier studies, suggested that the RIPK1–TAK1–NF-κB axis constitutes an essential scaffold platform necessary for the liver's adaptation to metabolic fluctuations.
evidence: This claim is based on the current study's findings combined with previous literature on TAK1 and NEMO.

claim: Both short-term fasting and HFD can increase FFA in the bloodstream, leading to their influx and accumulation in the liver.
source: Regarding the upstream signal of RIPK1, both short-term fasting and HFD can increase FFA in the bloodstream, leading to their influx and accumulation in the liver.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about lipid metabolism during fasting and HFD feeding.

claim: FFA accumulation in the liver may cause lipotoxicity in hepatocytes through ER stress.
source: This accumulation may cause lipotoxicity in hepatocytes through ER stress (Geng et al., 2021; Piccolis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Geng et al., 2021; Piccolis et al., 2019).

claim: The liver typically maintains immune tolerance and does not incite inflammation in response to various endogenous and exogenous PAMPs or antigens present in the bloodstream.
source: Moreover, in contrast to organs such as the small intestine and lungs, the liver typically maintains immune tolerance and does not incite inflammation in response to various endogenous and exogenous PAMPs or antigens present in the bloodstream.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about liver immunology.

claim: Hepatocyte RIPK1 serves as a critical mechanism for preserving immune tolerance within the liver microenvironment.
source: Our research revealed that hepatocyte RIPK1 serves as a critical mechanism for preserving immune tolerance within the liver microenvironment.
evidence: This claim is based on the finding that RIPK1 deficiency leads to inflammation during fasting, suggesting RIPK1 normally maintains immune tolerance.

claim: The physiological inflammation observed in RIPK1-deficient livers during short-term fasting is milder but akin to hepatic inflammation induced by pathogenic infections and other pathological conditions.
source: Furthermore, we identify an instance of physiological inflammation induced by loss of regulation in normal tissue. The physiological inflammation observed in RIPK1-deficient livers during short-term fasting is milder but akin to hepatic inflammation induced by pathogenic infections and other pathological conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that RIPK1-deficient livers show inflammatory responses during fasting that are similar to but milder than pathological inflammation.

claim: The physiological inflammation in RIPK1-deficient livers is characterized by the upregulation of typical molecules, including Ccl2, Tnfa, Ifng, Il6, and the recruitment of macrophages into liver tissue.
source: It is characterized by the upregulation of typical molecules, including Ccl2, Tnfa, Ifng, Il6, etc., and the recruitment of macrophages into liver tissue, indicating systemic adaptive responses.
evidence: This claim is based on the data showing increased inflammatory markers and macrophage recruitment in RIPK1-deficient livers during fasting.

claim: Deletion of RIPK1 in hepatocytes was confirmed by the analysis of RIPK1 expression in the liver tissue.
source: Deletion of RIPK1 in hepatocytes was confirmed by the analysis of RIPK1 expression in the liver tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents Western blot data confirming RIPK1 deletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Ripk1-hepKO mice were normal and healthy under steady conditions.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Filliol et al., 2016), Ripk1-hepKO mice were normal and healthy.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature (Filliol et al., 2016) and confirmed by the current study's observations.
